7.12.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint [13].

7.12.1.en: He hoped, as many people are accustomed to do, to find in sleep an escape from what had befallen him, and so he awaited the coming of night, that he might perhaps doze, if only for a while.

7.12.2.en: * In Holy Scripture the words "bed," "couch" or "cradle" made of the straw on which animals lie down are usually used to indicate the secrets of the depths of the heart. Therefore every single soul, pierced by the Bridegroom with the spears of holy love, says in the Song of Songs: "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth" (Song 3:1)...

7.12.3.en: So the Truth says to those who love Him: "The kingdom of God is within you" (Lk 17:21). Again: "If I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you" (Jn 16:7), as though saying plainly: "If I do not withdraw My body from your attention concentrated on it, I will not lead you by the Comforter, the Spirit, and you will perceive the invisible." Therefore it is said by the Psalmist of the righteous: "Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds" (Ps 149:5), since, fleeing from harm to outward things, they are glorified in peace within the depths of their hearts.

7.12.5.en: * This resembles the angels, who do not sleep because they are always standing on guard. Therefore you speak the truth, and so you imitate the angels who do not sleep and who do not flee from facing the truth by means of unreal fantasies.

7.12.6.en: * A man sleeps after he enters into a state of absence, and during sleep the food is digested and the health of those who share in the table of the feast is preserved. Therefore the bride sleeps after the feast. This sleep is considered unusual, and differs from ordinary sleep, in which the person is not unaware of what is around him. The two are opposed to one another, for sleeping and waking follow each other. And we see in the bride a distinctive mixture of opposites: she says, "I sleep, but my heart waketh" (Song 2:5). What do we understand from this verse? This sleep resembles death, in which all the functions of sensation cease: there is no sight, hearing, smell, taste or sense of touch, but the blood pressure falls. A person forgets anxiety during sleep, the passion of fear is calmed, anger diminishes and anxiety over bitter trials lessens, and it makes the person unaware of evils. Therefore we learn from the bride that she was lifted up and boasts, saying: "I sleep, but my heart waketh."

7.12.7.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * Cast off the sleep of heedlessness so that you may knock at the door of Christ. Paul asked that this door be opened to him to speak the mystery of Christ (Col 3:4); perhaps this is the door that John saw open: "After this I looked, and, behold, a door was opened in heaven: and the first voice which I heard was as it were of a trumpet talking with me; which said, Come up hither, and I will shew thee things which must be hereafter" (Rev 4:1). The door was opened to John and also to Paul, that they might receive for us loaves for our nourishment, because they persevered and knocked at the door in season and out of season (2 Tim 4:2), to restore life to the Gentiles who were weary and worn out from the way of the world with the abundance of heavenly food.

7.13.0.en: St. Ambrose Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions [14].

7.13.1.en: Night could not carry him away from weariness, nor sleep draw him out of distress; rather the dreams terrified him and the visions frightened him. The night became disturbing no less than the day.

7.13.2.en: We need the strong hand of God, who alone can keep us; behold our Keeper, who neither slumbers nor sleeps.

7.13.3.en: * What are we to understand here by dreams and visions but imaginings of the last examination at the judgment...

7.13.4.en: If dreams did not often bear deceptive images coming from our hidden enemy, the wise man would not refer to them by saying: [For dreams and vain imaginations have deceived many] (Sir 34:7).

7.14.0.en: So that my soul chooseth strangling, and death rather than my bones [15].

7.14.1.en: He did not care by what kind of death he died; what concerned him was that God would allow him to die. He does not seek deliverance from the affliction, but from temporal life as a whole.

7.14.2.en: I loathe it; I would not live alway.

7.15.0.en: Let me alone; for my days are vanity! [16]

7.15.1.en: Besides the calamities that befell the blessed Job, whether concerning his possessions, the death of his sons, or his wife's opposition to him, St. John Chrysostom adds the following things, which made the trial exceedingly bitter:

7.15.2.en: [First: his lack of certain knowledge about the Kingdom of Heaven and the resurrection, of which he rightly spoke with sorrow: [I shall not live forever, so I must endure much] (Job 16:7) LXX.

7.15.3.en: Second: his sense that he had done many good works.

7.15.4.en: Third: his sense that he had done no evil.

7.15.5.en: Fourth: his supposition that what had befallen him came from God's hands; for if it had been from the hands of Satan, this would have lessened his distress.

7.15.6.en: Fifth: his hearing from his friends, who accuse him of evil, saying: "God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" (Job 6:11).

7.15.7.en: Sixth: he sees those who live in evil in prosperity, and puffed up against him.

7.15.8.en: Seventh: he has no other before him to look to who has suffered such things.]

7.15.9.en: * [Let my life be freed from my spirit, and my soul from my body, and my bones from death. For I shall not live forever, so I am bound to endure patiently]... He had the desire to depart from here... until his body was dissolved. Job did not care about the stripping of his bones. Why is this? Because he says that the present life is quickly passing. "I shall not live alway." It is clear that Job is speaking of earthly life. How is he to be long-suffering in this matter? Only because the attainment of happiness requires long-suffering and patience, that is, the happiness to come... Job's speech clearly hints that material life is weak, corruptible, unstable, quickly passing, and does not bear the marks of eternal life.

7.16.s.en: 4. A cry to God for his deliverance

7.16.0.en: 17 What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? 18 And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment? 19 How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle? 20 I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself? 21 And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity? for now shall I sleep in the dust; and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I shall not be.

7.16.1.en: What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? [17]

7.16.2.en: In his distress Job felt that man is too trivial to be the object of God's regard, contention and testing. It is as though he says to God: Why do You occupy Yourself with so weak a creature? Why do You visit him from the morning and try him? He is too trivial to stand before You, utterly unable to enter the crucible of trials. The Psalmist says: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" (Ps 8:4).

7.16.3.en: Perhaps Job stood amazed before God's surpassing care for man; for despite man's weakness and lowliness, God is occupied with him, testing him in order to prove him and glorify him.

7.16.4.en: Job marvels that God sets His heart upon man so that he is dear to Him, like a person to whom He is tender, and makes a place for him in His divine heart. He visits him every morning with new mercies, as a friend takes care for his friend's love for him, or as a physician asks every morning about the state of his patient. And every moment He tests him, like one who feels his pulse and is jealous over him.

7.16.5.en: In his discourse on the creation of man, St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that God created the world with all artistry as a great palace prepared for Adam and Eve as king and queen. And that God offered man every possibility of happiness and authority over the creation that God brought into being for his sake.

7.16.6.en: In his discourse on true greatness and false greatness, St. Jacob of Sarug spoke creatively, bringing out God's surpassing love for man. He adorned the heavens with stars and prepared the earth with beautiful creatures, and gave both to man to be under his authority. God willed for man to be possessor of glory and authority, but through the envy of the devil he fell into false greatness, and so lost his true greatness. Yet God allowed Adam to return to what he had been, dust, not to humiliate him, but that he might not live forever having lost his greatness; rather, by discovering his true nature he receives glory through the work of the Savior.

7.16.7.en: * God glorifies man by enriching him with an abundance of the gift of reason, visits him by the inspiration of grace, and glorifies him by the greatness of the gift of virtue; for although he is nothing in himself, through the generosity of God's compassionate love He grants him to be a partaker in the knowledge of God Himself. The Lord sets His heart upon man, and thus glorifies him, and then brings him to judgment after He has given him His gifts, weighs his merits with precision, and with firmness judges the burdens of life, and brings precise punishment after he has been given many advantages.

7.16.9.en: * Which of the earthly creatures was created in the image of God except man?

7.16.10.en: And to whom was given authority over all nature and its creatures, to hold as his own?

7.16.11.en: It is an original honor that crowns his brow and exalts him to heaven, above the stars, loftier than the sun in majesty and dignity... And although he is lower in rank than the angels because of his attachment to a material body, he was granted power to understand and know his Lord and Creator.

7.16.12.en: St. Basil the Great * He stretched out the heavens, and set in them all the lights: the sun, the moon and all the stars, which move about in it.

7.16.13.en: The heavens did not ask, but He adorned them with fair sights that dazzle the eyes of beholders.

7.16.14.en: The sun has no mouth with which to ask for a great light to shine on all creation.

7.16.15.en: He adorned all kinds of birds and beasts with delightful and brilliant colors from the beginning.

7.16.16.en: He adorned creation, and in its perfection its adornment did not change.

7.16.17.en: He perfected the house of all creation, as it is said, and adorned it with beautiful forms.

7.16.18.en: The house stood, a building full of wonder.

7.16.19.en: He filled it all with beauty, with adornments that cannot be uttered.

7.16.20.en: And when He had perfected the house with all that is in it, the Maker sought to set in it one who is full of beauty.

7.16.21.en: He took dust and formed Adam, and breathed into his face the breath of life-giving life.

7.16.22.en: He perfected him, and he became a pattern full of wonder!

7.16.23.en: He made him in His likeness, and filled him with glory and splendor!

7.16.24.en: His light blazed, and the light of the sun went out before him because of the glory his Lord granted him when He created him.

7.16.25.en: St. Jacob of Sarug * Adam was not created to die, but to strive for immortality, and to show his trustworthiness. And to offer proof of it he added: [Who gave us the earnest of the Spirit](f)... And now He works through Baptism, and gives us a pledge that is not small: the Holy Spirit.

7.17.0.en: St. John Chrysostom And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment! [18]

7.17.1.en: * With what did David sing in similar terms? [Lord, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him? or the son of man, that thou makest account of him?] (Ps 144:3-4). Why did David say this about men, and what was his thought when he explained what follows: [Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away](g). Why in all truth does God glorify this weak man, and give him regard in the present state of evil? The righteous ask God because of their ignorance... For He is [the maker of good things and the lover of mankind](h) (Wis 7:22), and visits often the one He has created and gives him great attention. Therefore David also adds: "Bow thy heavens, O Lord, and come down" (Ps 144:5; 18:9). By this he shows God's intense concern for men, for in bowing the heavens He Himself comes down to us, "the Word was made flesh" (Jn 1:14); He shared our condition, strengthening and fortifying our weakness. As for Job, he shows at length how much good comes to the man whom God remembers.

7.17.2.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [And that thou shouldest visit him every dawn (morning), and try him suddenly] [18]... Night turns to light when the darkness of our error is lit by the knowledge of the truth. Night turns to light when the splendor of righteousness lights our hearts, which the dense blindness of sin had covered. Paul saw the dawn appear in the minds of the disciples when he said: "The night is far spent, the day is at hand" (Rom 13:12).

7.17.3.en: But let us note that after God visits man at dawn, He tries him suddenly; for by His approach He lifts our hearts to the virtuous heights, and when He withdraws He allows him to be attacked by temptation. After receiving the gifts of the virtues, if the soul is not stirred by the assault of temptation it becomes puffed up, and thinks that what it has received is from itself...

7.17.4.en: So Elijah was visited at dawn, and he opened the doors of heaven with a word, but immediately he was tried, and fled to the wilderness as one without help, for fear of a lone woman (1 Kgs 19:1-3).

7.17.5.en: And so Paul, when he was caught up to the third heaven and penetrated the mysteries of paradise, received contemplation. Yet when he returned to himself he wrestled against the assaults of the flesh, and was subjected to another law in his members, and was grieved by its rebellion, seeing that the law of the Spirit was threatened (2 Cor 12:2 etc.).

7.18.0.en: How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle? [19]

7.18.1.en: He asks God to lift His rod from him, if only for moments, that he may breathe.

7.18.2.en: St. John Chrysostom, in his treatise "Divine Providence," dealt with the problem of those who stumble in the love of God because of the afflictions that befall them:

7.18.3.en: * Let us then hasten to correct those who stumble because of affliction, forgetting God's providence and love, and spare them from falling under this penalty, making clear to them the cause of their sickness.

7.18.4.en: What is the cause of this great danger: disregard of God's providence?!

7.18.5.en: It is rashness and curiosity of thought. It is the desire to understand all the causes of the events that befall us, and the wish to contend against God's providence, which cannot be comprehended nor described, that providence which surpasses all examination and investigation! Yet man is not ashamed of this curious attitude, full of recklessness.

7.18.6.en: Who, then, surpassed Paul in wisdom? Tell me, was he not a chosen vessel? Did he not receive the surpassing grace of the Spirit, which cannot be uttered? Did not Christ speak in him? Did not God reveal to him things that cannot be uttered? Did he not hear what it is not lawful for a man to utter? Was he not caught up into paradise and lifted up to the third heaven?(i) Did he not traverse seas and land, drawing pagans to Christianity? Did he not receive the various gifts of the Spirit...? And with all this, this man, with his greatness, wisdom, power and fullness of the Spirit, since God favored him with these privileges, when he looks at God's providence, not in all its aspects but in one aspect of it, is overcome by the call, crushed, and quickly draws back, submitting to the incomprehensible God. For he did not search into God's providence for the angels, nor the archangels, or the Cherubim and Seraphim and all the invisible orders, nor into His care for the sun and the moon, the heaven, the earth and the sea, nor into His watchfulness over the whole human race and His concern for the irrational animals, the crops, the grass, the winds, the springs and the rivers... but God's special providence for the Jews and the Greeks, and he enlarged on the point, and explained how God called the Gentiles and rejected the Jews, and then showed how He accomplished salvation... And when he comprehended this, the Apostle discovered that he was before a vast ocean, and as he tried to examine the depths of this providence he trembled, realizing the impossibility of explaining its causes, and was awed before His infinite providence, which is unbounded, indescribable, unsearchable and incomprehensible, and he drew back in reverence, marveling, and saying: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" (Rom 11:33).

7.18.7.en: He then showed how he touched its depths without succeeding in searching them out, saying: "How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!"

7.18.8.en: He did not say only that His judgments are unsearchable, but that they are also past finding out. Not only is man unable to understand them, but he has no right even to begin to search them out. It is impossible for him to grasp their end or even to discover the beginning of their design?!

7.18.9.en: And having said "How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out," he ended his discourse, filled with wonder and trembling, with a hymn of thanksgiving, saying: [For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen].

7.18.10.en: St. John Chrysostom I have sinned;

7.18.11.en: what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?

7.19.0.en: Why hast thou set me as a mark against thee (why hast thou made me a target for thee), so that I am a burden to myself! [20]

7.19.1.en: God bore witness of Job that he was perfect and upright, but Job confesses that he is a sinner. He says "Have I sinned?" or "I have sinned." If before his friends he declares that he is innocent, and has not committed one of the heinous sins which the friends perhaps thought he had committed in secret, yet before God he declares that he will not be justified before Him, because he sins. How can he justify himself before God "the preserver of men," who knows what is in their hearts and thoughts and is concerned with their holiness and purity.

7.19.2.en: Job declares before God his inability to act: he has sinned, but what can he do for God? There is no one who can satisfy divine justice, but we ask for His mercies, and hide under the shadow of His wings, and prepare ourselves for the work of His grace, and so become the object of His good pleasure.

7.19.3.en: * He says: [If I have sinned, what shall I do, O You who perceive the mind of men?] [20] Are You not the one who called me [blameless, truly, righteous, godly, with no evil in me?] (Job 1:8; 2:3). You did not give this testimony out of ignorance, for You know man entirely, since You created what is within him and what is outside; but if those who revile and despise me, saying that I am a sinner, make light of my righteous deeds, which qualified me for Your testimony, what shall I do?

7.19.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * He says this not to accuse God personally, God forbid! but because what had befallen him gave rise to a great accusation against God.

7.19.5.en: Therefore he says: [You perceive the mind of men]. For even if they do not speak, You know their secret thoughts, all their personal reflections.

7.19.6.en: Such a man has endured much. For he did not say: "I am righteous," but said: They have a good idea of me. See, they bring an accusation against You because of my trials.

7.19.7.en: St. John Chrysostom And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity? for now shall I sleep in the dust;

7.20.0.en: and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I shall not be! [21]

7.20.1.en: In fervent prayer he cried out asking for forgiveness: "Why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity?" It is clear that he did not ask merely for temporal rest and for the trial to be lifted from him, but asks for God's favor, that his inner joy might be restored to him.

7.20.2.en: He asks for forgiveness now while he is in the world, because if he dies and lies in the dust there is no place for repentance, and his relation with God is cut off.

7.20.3.en: * By these very words, what does he declare but the desire for the expected Mediator, of whom John says: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29). Or rather, sin is taken away completely from mankind when our corruption is changed into the glory of incorruption.

7.20.4.en: For we can never be freed from sin as long as we are held in the mortal body. Therefore the person longs for the grace of the Savior for the perfection of the resurrection, when the person looks upon evil as having utterly passed away. Therefore immediately after speaking of the punishment he deserved (through his inheritance from Adam) and the judgment he dreads because of his deeds, he continues: [Now I shall sleep in the dust, you will seek me in the morning, and I shall not be]. It was said to the first man when he sinned: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19). Now in the morning, that is, in the revealing of souls, when thoughts become naked at the coming of the Judge, light comes in place of the darkness of night. The Psalmist said of this: [In the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up] (Ps 5:3).

7.20.6.en: * I, the sinner, always need healing.

7.20.7.en: * Whenever we receive it (in Communion) we proclaim the death of the Lord. By the death we proclaim the forgiveness of sins. If the shedding of blood is for the forgiveness of sins, it is fitting for me always to receive it, that it may always forgive my sins.

7.20.8.en: St. Ambrose * That you are called a man is the work of God, and that you are called a sinner is the work of man himself.

7.20.9.en: Blot out what you have done, that God may save what He has made.

7.20.10.en: It is fitting for you to hate your own work in you, and to love God's work in you.

7.20.11.en: When your own works do not please you, in this God's good works begin, since you find fault with your evil works.

7.20.12.en: The confession of evil works is the beginning of good works.

7.20.13.en: You do the truth and come to the light. How do you do the truth? You do not pamper yourself, nor humor yourself, nor flatter yourself, nor say: "I am righteous," while you are not righteous; thus you begin to do the truth.

7.20.14.en: You come to the light that your works may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God, because your sin, the very thing you hate, you cannot hate unless God shines in you and the truth shows it to you.

7.20.15.en: But whoever loves his sins even after being admonished, hates the light that admonishes him and flees from it, for the works he loves do not appear to him to be evil. He who does the truth accuses his evil works in himself and does not justify himself, and does not pardon himself until God forgives him.

7.20.16.en: So whoever wishes God to forgive him knows his sins himself and comes to the light, where he gives thanks for the showing of what he must hate in himself. He says to God: "Hide thy face from my sins." But with what face does he say this unless he adds: [For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me] (Ps 51:11)?

7.20.17.en: Let your iniquities be before you, you who do not wish them to be before God.

7.20.18.en: But if you put your sins behind you, God will push them forward and set them before your eyes, and this will happen at a time when there is no longer any fruit of repentance.

7.20.20.en: Our days are an unceasing trial

7.20.21.en: * What do I see in my life upon earth?

7.20.23.en: I live like the hireling who awaits the end of the day, to rest from his toil and receive wages for his living.

7.20.24.en: * The day with all its hardship hands me over to the night, and the night with its terror hands me over to the day.

7.20.25.en: When shall I find my rest?

7.20.26.en: The months of my life hasten me to my departure.

7.20.27.en: The days of my sojourn pass quickly like vapor, they pass and are scattered without return!

7.20.28.en: * If I go down to Hades I do not return to life on earth, and my dwelling place on the face of the earth no longer knows me * In the midst of afflictions I cry out: Who am I, dust and ashes, that You should care for me and discipline me?

7.20.29.en: Who am I, a creature of dust, that You should visit me?

7.20.30.en: * You are my hope, my joy and my treasure!

7.20.31.en: In You I do not fear death; in You my wearisome journey is turned into a joyful passage!

7.20.32.en: Accompany me on the way of my sufferings, and my sorrows will turn into unceasing songs and praises!
